r: EXS 1020 teaches students to execute and self-correct resistance-training technique — grip, joint alignment, range of motion — through direct physical practice tied to muscle anatomy, mapping to O*NET's Performing General Physical Activities and Monitoring Processes activities rather than any knowledge-work category. Task-exposure research consistently places manual, real-time physical skill acquisition among the least-exposed activity clusters, and no institutional mandate governs the course; its protection comes entirely from embodiment. AI form-analysis apps already exist, but they assist an instructor's eye rather than substitute for a student physically learning to execute a lift safely. At 24 months, verification of technique is still best done by a human coach watching a live body move, since improper form carries real injury risk. The instrumental need to physically practice resistance training is essentially untouched by current AI capability; the course is not a knowledge-transmission exercise but a motor-skill one.

By 2031, AI-powered video-based movement analysis will likely be more capable and more available in gyms and apps, and some programming guidance may shift toward algorithmic recommendation. That still does not perform the psychomotor learning this course targets: a student must personally acquire safe lifting mechanics under supervision, and correcting a joint-alignment error in real time remains an embodied, in-person judgment call. Task-exposure research's finding that manual physical-skill work is comparatively immune to language-model substitution continues to apply across this horizon, and diffusion data show AI adoption in physical-training settings remains uneven even as capability advances. No accreditation or licensure structure locks the course in place, but none is needed — the protection is structural, coming from what the course actually teaches. The rating holds Low; better AI coaching tools augment the instructor, they do not remove the requirement that a student build the physical skill themselves.

A decade out, motion-capture and AI coaching feedback could be commonplace in resistance-training settings, and the METR/Epoch capability trend suggests substantially more sophisticated real-time movement analysis by 2036. Even so, the central case still has a human physically performing and refining a lift under supervision — embodiment is not a temporary bottleneck that capability erodes, it is definitional to what the course is teaching. Verification of safe technique for a live human body remains a real-time, in-person judgment task regardless of how good AI's descriptive feedback becomes. The wider uncertainty concerns how much AI-generated coaching content supplements instruction, not whether students still need to practice the movements themselves. The rating stays Low with reasonable confidence; the course's psychomotor core sits about as far from AI's actual substitution frontier as any activity in the catalog.
EXS 1020.d: This is an introductory course that will allow students to enhance their knowledge and experience regarding resistance training. Regardless of experience, all students will learn proper exercise technique and terminology (through skill analysis and muscle anatomy) and basic resistance training programing methods. This course is not designed to help the student design resistance training programs for other individuals.

r: EXS 1640 combines hands-on practice in strength, endurance, flexibility, and body-composition assessment with exercise prescription and leadership skills exercised through active participation — a blend of applied physical activity and program administration mapped to O*NET's Performing General Physical Activities and Coaching and Developing Others. The administrative layer (writing basic prescriptions) is more exposed than the practical layer, since task-exposure research finds programming and template-generation tasks more automatable than physical, in-person coaching. But the course's graded competence is demonstrated leadership and hands-on delivery, which stays low-exposure. No general-studies or accreditation mandate applies, so protection here rests on embodiment rather than institutional lock-in. At 24 months, AI can draft a generic fitness plan, but it cannot lead active participation or correct a student's exercise administration technique in real time. The instrumental need to build this hands-on capability is not eroded.

By 2031, AI fitness-programming tools will likely generate more sophisticated exercise prescriptions on demand, further automating the administrative portion of the course's content. That erodes the case for teaching manual program-writing in isolation, but the course's core deliverable — leading active participation and demonstrating fitness techniques in person — remains an embodied, real-time activity that a generated program cannot perform on the student's behalf. Diffusion data indicate AI adoption in fitness settings, while growing, remains uneven across firms and instructional contexts. Verification of correct technique during active leadership still requires a present, trained human. With no institutional lock-in to fall back on, the rating depends entirely on this embodiment dampener, which continues to hold at 5 years. The instrumental case shifts modestly toward AI-assisted program drafting, but the leadership and hands-on delivery skills the course targets remain necessary.

A decade out, AI program generation for general fitness populations may be close to fully automated, and capability growth broadly, per the METR/Epoch task-horizon trend, makes this plausible well before 2036. Yet the course's applied core — leading fitness activity and demonstrating technique to real participants — is not delegable in the same way; embodiment continues to dampen the rating even as the prescription-writing task itself becomes trivially automatable. The genuine uncertainty is how much of the course's content shifts toward directing AI-generated programs versus continuing to teach manual prescription-writing, not whether hands-on leadership skill remains necessary. Absent any accreditation floor, the rating rests on the durability of in-person coaching demand. The rating holds Low, though with somewhat less confidence than 1020, since the administrative half of this course is more exposed than its purely psychomotor counterpart.
EXS 1640.d: Students in this course will be introduced to basic skills, practice, and theory in physical fitness. Major components of muscular strength, muscular endurance, cardiovascular endurance, flexibility, and body composition are discussed. Exercise prescription, administration and leadership skills are enhanced through active participation.

r: Group Exercise Leadership develops live coaching competence: selecting exercises, identifying improper form across a group in real time, and demonstrating modifications for a room of participants with mixed skill and injury risk. This maps directly to O*NET's Coaching and Developing Others and Establishing and Maintaining Interpersonal Relationships activities — precisely the categories task-exposure research places among the least automatable, since they require synchronous physical presence and rapid interpersonal judgment. AI can generate a class format or playlist, but it cannot read a room, spot a participant about to injure themselves, or adapt cueing on the fly. Verification of safe form for multiple simultaneous bodies is an inherently embodied task. At 24 months the instrumental need to build this specific live-leadership competence is fully intact; no institutional mandate is needed to protect it because embodiment alone does the work.

By 2031, AI will likely produce more sophisticated class programming and even personalized cueing scripts, but the graded skill in this course — leading a live group safely and adaptively — remains an in-person, real-time activity outside language-model substitution. Task-exposure research's finding that physically synchronous, interpersonal coaching work resists automation continues to hold, and the productivity gains documented elsewhere for AI-assisted work in writing or coding contexts simply do not transfer to simultaneous multi-person physical instruction. Diffusion of AI tools into fitness-class settings is real but uneven, and none of it substitutes for the instructor's embodied presence. The rating stays Low; whatever planning assistance AI offers an instructor preparing a class, the instrumental need for a student to develop live group-leadership skill through this course is essentially unaffected.

Ten years out, even substantial capability growth does not change the fundamental character of group exercise leadership as synchronous, embodied, safety-critical human coaching. AI may become a capable co-planner for class structure and music, and generative tools will likely be routine in fitness businesses by 2036, but the moment-to-moment task this course trains — reading multiple live bodies and adjusting instruction accordingly — has no digital substitute a participant would accept in place of a present instructor. The wide uncertainty in this horizon concerns how the fitness industry packages AI-assisted programming around instructors, not whether the embodied leadership skill remains instrumentally necessary. The rating holds Low with high confidence, anchored in the same embodiment logic that protects the course at 24 months and 5 years.
EXS 2680.d: Students in this course will expand their knowledge and skills in performance techniques, program design, and leadership needed to teach small group exercise programs or group-led exercise classes for healthy adults. Students will become familiar with coaching a variety of group fitness formats intended to enhance cardiorespiratory fitness, muscle strength and endurance, and musculoskeletal flexibility. Students will develop the ability to select appropriate exercises, identify improper form/technique, recommend/demonstrate appropriate exercise progression, and modify exercises based on skill and/or to minimize injury.

r: This course orients students to the personal-training profession through business elements — settings, client acquisition, professional practice — alongside hands-on exercise lessons and demonstrations, with program design explicitly de-emphasized. The business-orientation content, understanding markets and client-facing professional norms, maps to more exposed O*NET categories like Getting Information and Organizing Work, while the hands-on demonstration component sits in low-exposure physical-coaching territory. Observed-usage data shows office and informational tasks are where AI use concentrates most heavily, which pushes exposure up for the business half, but the course's applied hands-on lessons keep the graded competence partly embodied. No accreditation body governs exercise-science curricula, so the rating rests on this embodiment residue rather than institutional lock-in. At 24 months, AI can explain personal-training business models fluently, but it does not replace a student practicing hands-on client-facing training.

By 2031, AI business-planning and marketing tools will likely handle much of the informational content this course currently teaches about running a personal-training practice — client acquisition strategy, business structuring, professional messaging. That erodes the informational half of the course meaningfully. What remains resistant is the hands-on demonstration and in-person professional-presence component, which stays embodied and interpersonal regardless of how capable AI business tools become. Diffusion of AI into small fitness-business operations is plausible but uneven by this horizon. Because the hands-on residue is real, though modest, the dampener continues to apply and the rating stays Low rather than climbing with the informational content's exposure. The instrumental case shifts toward using AI for the business-planning work while still requiring embodied training practice, which is what keeps a student enrolled in this specific course.

A decade out, AI will plausibly be a capable business advisor and client-communication drafter for personal trainers, substantially eroding the informational rationale for the course's non-hands-on content. The applied, in-person training-demonstration component, however, remains a task AI does not perform on the student's behalf, and that embodied residue is what keeps the overall rating from rising. The uncertainty is real about how personal training as a profession restructures around AI-assisted business operations by 2036, but that is a labor-market question distinct from whether a student preparing to train clients still needs hands-on practice. The rating holds Low, with the acknowledgment that this course's business-content half is considerably more exposed than its practical-demonstration half, making it a genuinely mixed case within the exercise-science curriculum.
EXS 2890.d: This class is designed to introduce students to the personal training profession from a variety of perspectives. While program design and training techniques will be presented, these concepts are not the focus of the course. Emphasis will be placed on an exploration of the various settings where personal training services are offered and the business elements that all professional personal trainers should comprehend. Class discussions, lectures, hands-on exercise lessons and demonstrations will help students gain a greater awareness of what it takes to be a competent, professional personal trainer.

r: This course teaches fitness professionals to adapt exercise prescription for medically complex populations — diabetes, asthma, metabolic disorder, anxiety, multiple sclerosis, arthritis — a knowledge-application task closer to clinical decision support than hands-on coaching, mapping to O*NET's Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance and Making Decisions and Solving Problems. That analytical character makes it more exposed than the resistance-training and group-leadership courses in this sequence: task-exposure research finds informational, prescriptive knowledge work meaningfully more automatable than embodied physical instruction. The binding constraint is verification burden rather than embodiment or accreditation — a wrong exercise recommendation for someone with a cardiac or metabolic condition carries real, non-obvious harm, exactly the adversarial error-cost profile that keeps a trained human in the loop. At 24 months, AI can suggest generic modifications, but the instrumental need for a student to learn condition-specific clinical judgment is intact.

By 2031, AI decision-support tools will plausibly generate condition-adjusted exercise recommendations with real sophistication, and observed-usage data already shows this kind of information-synthesis task among AI's most common applications. That materially erodes the course's execution rationale — producing a modified program becomes something AI does competently. What survives is the verification layer: the jagged-frontier finding that AI users outside a model's competence zone are meaningfully less accurate, and that mis-calibrated trust is a real risk, applies directly here, since a subtle contraindication for a special-population client is exactly the kind of non-obvious failure a novice could miss. The rating rises to Medium: the instrumental case shifts from generating recommendations to critically evaluating and adapting AI-suggested ones for medically complex clients, a competence this course still needs to teach directly.

A decade out, AI exercise-prescription tools for special populations will likely be capable and widely diffused in clinical and fitness settings alike, substantially eroding the case for teaching manual prescription-writing as the course's central task. But the verification burden does not disappear — a fitness professional working with clients who have cardiovascular, metabolic, or neurological conditions still needs the clinical literacy to recognize when an AI-generated recommendation is unsafe, an oversight role task-exposure research suggests grows more valuable as generation itself commoditizes. The rating holds Medium rather than rising further, capped by this durable verification requirement. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much of the course shifts toward AI-output evaluation versus original prescription design, not whether condition-specific clinical judgment remains instrumentally necessary for this population.
EXS 3780.d: This course is designed to help fitness professionals adapt exercise prescription to meet the needs of people with special exercise requirements. Special populations may include people with diabetes, asthma, metabolic disorder, anxiety, multiple sclerosis and arthritis, as examples.

r: This course addresses physiological, cognitive, and psychological change across the lifespan and applies that knowledge to exercise assessment and prescription for chronic conditions like metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular disease, osteoporosis, and neurological decline — squarely an information-synthesis and clinical-judgment task, mapping to O*NET's Evaluating Information to Determine Compliance and Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others. This informational character is more exposed than the hands-on courses earlier in the sequence, consistent with task-exposure research's finding that knowledge-synthesis work automates more readily than embodied physical coaching. The binding constraint is verification burden: prescribing exercise for a frail older adult with osteoporosis or a child with a developmental condition carries real, non-obvious injury risk if misjudged, which keeps a trained human necessary. At 24 months the instrumental need to build lifespan-specific clinical judgment is intact despite the content's inherent exposure.

By 2031, AI will likely generate competent lifespan-adjusted exercise guidance drawing on physiological and developmental literature, and observed-usage data shows this kind of applied-knowledge synthesis among AI's most common uses. The execution rationale for manually producing these recommendations erodes accordingly. What remains necessary is evaluative: recognizing when a generated recommendation misjudges a specific child's developmental stage or an older adult's comorbidity profile, exactly the kind of non-obvious failure the jagged-frontier research warns about when users operate outside a model's reliable zone. The rating rises to Medium, driven by real erosion in the content-generation task but capped by this verification requirement. The instrumental case increasingly centers on critically checking AI-generated lifespan programming rather than producing it from scratch, a shift the course would need to reflect but that does not remove its necessity.

A decade out, AI tools tailored to pediatric and geriatric exercise physiology will likely be broadly capable, further eroding the rationale for teaching manual, from-scratch program design across the lifespan. The clinical-judgment residue persists, however: working safely with children and older or medically fragile adults carries genuine error costs, and the verification competence this course builds remains necessary even as generation automates. The rating holds Medium, capped by that dampener rather than climbing toward High. The considerable uncertainty concerns how heavily lifespan exercise programming becomes AI-mediated in practice by 2036, but the underlying need for someone trained to catch an unsafe recommendation for a vulnerable population does not appear to disappear under any plausible central-case capability trajectory, and the course's role in building that judgment plausibly grows more, not less, important as generation itself becomes routine.
EXS 3790.d: The course is designed to introduce students to physiological, cognitive and psychological changes that occur from birth through adolescence and in the later stages of life. The role of physical activity and exercise will be explored in each of these life stages. Considerations for exercise assessment and prescriptions will be addressed for a number of chronic conditions, such as but not limited to: metabolic syndrome, diabetes, cardiovascular, osteoporosis, and neurological conditions.

r: This course compares current fitness-industry trends, evaluation programs, and certification pathways, and prepares students for employment through resume writing and interview skills — a largely informational, comparative, and writing-centered curriculum with minimal hands-on component, distinct from the practicum-heavy courses elsewhere in the sequence. That maps to O*NET's Documenting/Recording Information and Getting Information activities, categories observed-usage data shows are among AI's most common applications, and task-exposure research finds writing and informational-comparison tasks strongly positively associated with exposure. Neither embodiment nor verification burden substantially protects this content: comparing certification programs or drafting a resume carries low error cost and no adversarial stakes. No accreditation or general-studies mandate applies. At 24 months, AI already competently drafts comparative analyses and resumes, meaningfully eroding the course's execution rationale even this early, which pushes the rating to Medium.

By 2031, AI will very plausibly perform comparative industry analysis, certification research, and career-document drafting at a level approaching professional competence — the kind of gain professional-writing productivity studies already document, where AI assistance cuts drafting time substantially while improving output quality. With no embodiment, verification burden, or institutional lock protecting this content, the applied tasks the course teaches become broadly automatable by this horizon. The rating rises to High: a student can direct AI to produce a comparative program analysis or a polished resume competently, leaving little residual instrumental case for manual execution. What plausibly survives is career judgment and interview performance, both live and interpersonal, but that is a modest fraction of the course's actual content, and diffusion of these tools into fitness-industry career services is already plausible well within this horizon.

A decade out, AI-generated comparative analysis, certification research, and career-document preparation should be routine and highly capable, consistent with the sustained capability growth documented in task-time-horizon trends. The course's core deliverables — written comparison, career materials — are squarely inside AI's likely competence frontier by 2036, with no accreditation floor or embodiment residue to hold the rating down. The rating stays High, hedged by genuine uncertainty about how quickly fitness-industry credentialing itself evolves and by the live-interview component that remains human. Among the exercise-science courses in this batch, this is the clearest case of a course whose applied tasks sit squarely in AI's demonstrated strengths — informational synthesis and written production — rather than its acknowledged weaknesses in embodied, real-time physical instruction.
EXS 3841.d: In this course students will explore: 1) current trends, issues, and environments in fitness management, 2) comparison of selected popular fitness and evaluation programs, 3) certification programs and employment available for fitness personnel. Students will be provided opportunity for on-site visitations of selected exercise science work places as well as future employment preparation (e.g. resume writing and interviewing skills).

r: This course teaches interpretation of electrocardiograms — identifying atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, ischemia, and infarction — alongside hands-on cardiovascular physical exam and exercise-assessment skills. ECG interpretation is a pattern-recognition, diagnostic task, mapping to O*NET's Interpreting the Meaning of Information for Others and Analyzing Data or Information, categories where automated and AI-assisted interpretation already exist in clinical cardiology and are actively improving. That gives this course meaningfully higher base exposure than the hands-on courses elsewhere in the sequence. The binding constraint is verification burden, not embodiment: misreading a cardiac arrhythmia or infarction pattern has severe, non-obvious consequences, the exact adversarial error-cost profile the jagged-frontier research flags as requiring a knowledgeable human check. At 24 months the instrumental need to build ECG-reading competence directly is intact, since automated interpretation still requires expert oversight in this domain.

By 2031, AI-assisted ECG interpretation will likely be considerably more capable and more widely deployed in cardiovascular assessment settings, consistent with capability trends showing steady growth in structured pattern-recognition tasks. The execution rationale for a student manually reading every waveform erodes accordingly. What remains necessary is the verification competence: identifying when an automated read is wrong on a genuinely ambiguous tracing, a non-obvious-failure scenario that keeps expert human judgment load-bearing even as baseline accuracy improves. The rating rises to Medium, reflecting real exposure growth in the interpretive task capped by this durable verification requirement. The course's hands-on physical-exam component provides a secondary, modest protective residue, but the primary dampener here is the clinical stakes of misreading a life-threatening cardiac pattern.

A decade out, automated ECG interpretation should be highly capable and standard in most clinical and fitness-assessment workflows, substantially eroding the case for teaching manual waveform-reading as the course's central skill. Yet exercise physiologists and fitness professionals working with at-risk populations still need the clinical literacy to catch a dangerous misclassification, and that verification role does not shrink merely because baseline interpretation automates — if anything, the jagged-frontier finding about miscalibrated trust in AI outputs suggests it grows more important. The rating holds Medium, capped by verification burden rather than climbing to High. The uncertainty is in how the course balances teaching manual interpretation against teaching AI-output evaluation by 2036, not in whether cardiac-pattern literacy remains instrumentally necessary for this specialization.
EXS 4650.d: This course is designed to provide students with an overview of the basic interpretation of an electrocardiogram (ECG). Emphasis will be placed on identification of atrial and ventricular arrhythmias, myocardial ischemia and infarction. Students will become versed in components of cardiovascular physical exam as well as different cardiovascular exercise assessments.

r: This capstone-style course requires students to conduct hands-on fitness assessments using contemporary equipment and to demonstrate exercise-prescription competence through practical skills tests — an explicitly embodied, practicum-based course rather than a lecture on theory. That maps to O*NET's Performing General Physical Activities and Monitoring Processes or Surroundings, categories task-exposure research places firmly among the least automatable, since the graded competence is physically administering an assessment and observing a live physiological response, not producing a written prescription in isolation. Verification burden compounds the protection: an assessment error with a real client carries injury risk. No accreditation mandate governs exercise science, so the protection here is entirely structural. At 24 months, AI can help draft a prescription template, but it cannot administer the physical assessment or read a participant's real-time physiological response.

By 2031, AI will likely generate more sophisticated prescription output once assessment data is entered, but the practical-skills-test core of this course — physically conducting the assessment and interpreting a live response — remains embodied in a way that data-processing automation does not touch. Diffusion of AI-assisted fitness technology into assessment settings is plausible but does not substitute for the hands-on administration itself, and Census BTOS diffusion data suggest such adoption remains uneven across firms and practice settings at this horizon. Task-exposure research's consistent finding that physically-administered, real-time monitoring work resists substitution continues to apply. The rating stays Low: the analytical prescription-writing layer becomes more automatable, but the course's actual graded output — demonstrated competence conducting assessments on a live person — is not something a language model performs on the student's behalf.

A decade out, even considerable capability growth in AI-driven prescription generation, consistent with the METR/Epoch task-horizon trend, does not change the embodied character of physically administering a fitness assessment and demonstrating competence on a practical skills test. The instrumental need for a student to acquire this hands-on assessment capability persists in the central case through 2036, since the task is defined by physical execution and real-time observation of a live body, not by producing an output that a model could generate instead. The honest uncertainty concerns how much equipment and workflow becomes AI-augmented, not whether the practicum itself remains necessary. The rating holds Low with high confidence, consistent with the pattern across this batch's other hands-on assessment and practica courses.
EXS 4680.d: Students in this course will be acquainted with the art and science of exercise fitness assessment and exercise prescription. Students will evaluate the physiological responses to different physical fitness assessments using contemporary techniques and equipment. After completing the class, students will be expected to be competent to conduct fitness assessments and to prepare exercise prescriptions for a variety of populations. Practical skills tests to demonstrate each student's competence in these areas will be required.

r: This advanced course pairs conceptual content — biomechanics and exercise-physiology principles behind resistance training — with hands-on instruction in the technique and mechanical characteristics of advanced weight-training exercises for athletic populations, plus goal-oriented program design. The technique-and-mechanics component is embodied psychomotor coaching, mapping to O*NET's Training and Teaching Others and Coaching and Developing Others, categories task-exposure research places among the least exposed. The program-design component is somewhat more exposed, echoing the pattern in EXS 1640, but the graded core of this capstone course is demonstrated coaching competence on complex, injury-prone lifts, where verification burden is real — a misjudged cue on an advanced lift has real injury consequences. No accreditation mandate applies. At 24 months, the instrumental need to build hands-on advanced coaching competence is intact.

By 2031, AI will likely generate more sophisticated goal-oriented strength programs on demand, further automating the planning component of this course. That does not touch its embodied core: teaching a student to coach and execute advanced, biomechanically demanding lifts safely for athletic populations requires physical demonstration and real-time correction that a generated program cannot substitute for. The jagged-frontier finding about elevated error rates when users operate outside a model's reliable competence zone is directly relevant here, since advanced lifting technique errors are exactly the non-obvious-failure category with real injury cost. The rating stays Low: program-writing automates meaningfully, but the coaching and technique-demonstration skill this advanced course is built around remains an embodied, in-person competence that no amount of programming-side capability growth substitutes for.

A decade out, AI-generated strength-and-conditioning programming for athletic populations will plausibly be sophisticated and widely diffused, consistent with the sustained capability trend in task-time-horizon research, but the course's central task — coaching complex, biomechanically demanding lifts to athletes with real injury risk if mis-executed — stays embodied and resistant to substitution regardless of how good the underlying program generation becomes. The instrumental case for hands-on advanced coaching competence persists in the central case through 2036. The genuine uncertainty concerns how much of the planning and periodization work shifts to AI-assisted tools, not whether a strength-and-conditioning specialist still needs to personally develop and demonstrate advanced coaching technique. The rating holds Low, consistent with the embodiment-driven pattern across this batch's hands-on coaching and practicum courses.
EXS 4772.d: Students in this course will identify and elaborate upon important concepts from basic resistance training technique to biomechanics and exercise physiology. Students will design appropriate goal-oriented strength and power training programs for specific athletic populations. Students will also learn about the technique and mechanical characteristics of several advanced weight training exercises commonly used in athletic populations and other fitness programs.

r: Community Fitness Testing and Program Planning centers on conducting laboratory fitness assessments such as strength, flexibility, body-composition, and cardiovascular testing, then evaluating results, writing individualized exercise prescriptions, and promoting fitness programs. Administering these assessments requires a human physically present with equipment and a client, an embodied task current models cannot perform remotely. Observed-usage data from the Anthropic Economic Index shows heavy AI use concentrated in writing and office tasks, so the marketing and documentation pieces are already assisted, but that leaves the hands-on testing core untouched. Diffusion data from Census BTOS shows only a modest share of US firms have adopted AI tools at all, so even where digital sub-tasks are automatable, uptake among community fitness employers by 2028 remains limited. The binding constraint is embodiment: physically administering the tests is the course's instrumental core, and that resists remote substitution over this near horizon.

By 2031, the evaluative and program-design half of this course grows more exposed. Task-exposure research finds programming and writing tasks strongly positively associated with exposure, and generating an exercise prescription from test scores increasingly resembles a templated writing task that algorithmic fitness platforms already approximate; productivity studies on professional writing show large time savings alongside quality gains, suggesting program-planning documentation and marketing copy will be substantially AI-assisted by this horizon. Still, the course's defining activity, physically conducting the assessment battery, calipers, treadmills, dynamometers, with a live client, remains embodied and is not credibly displaced by five years given current diffusion rates. Verification burden is moderate rather than low since misapplied prescriptions carry real but usually recoverable risk. The instrumental need for supervised, in-person assessment training keeps this course's automation exposure capped below what the digital sub-tasks alone would suggest.

Ten years out, capability trends (METR/Epoch task-horizon doubling, roughly 4-7 months) suggest AI systems will competently handle program design, marketing, and outcome interpretation with little friction, and the GDPval finding that top models already approach expert-level performance on realistic deliverables supports treating those sub-tasks as largely automatable by 2036. Wearable sensors and computer-vision movement tracking could plausibly narrow the embodied core further, letting a trainer supervise AI-guided testing rather than perform every measurement personally. However, this is a hedge, not a confident prediction: adoption among community fitness and wellness employers has historically lagged capability, and hands-on client assessment retains a supervisory, safety-relevant role that resists full remote substitution. The course's instrumental exposure rises meaningfully but stops short of eliminating the need for trained, embodied assessment competency.
EXS 4780.d: This course is designed to provide the student with the opportunity to conduct laboratory fitness assessments, evaluate test results and develop exercise prescriptions. In addition, the student will become knowledgeable with regard to the promotion and marketing of fitness programs.

r: Special Considerations for Exercise Assessment and Prescription addresses exercise testing and prescription for clients with cardiovascular, metabolic, neurological, aging-related, or pregnancy-related conditions, requiring real-time monitoring of symptoms and vitals during physical exertion. This is high-stakes clinical judgment applied to medically complex populations, and the jagged-frontier research on AI use is directly relevant: outside a model's competence frontier, AI-assisted users are markedly less accurate while remaining overconfident, and miscalibrated trust in an AI-generated prescription for a cardiac or pregnant client carries genuine harm potential. The verification burden is high because errors are non-obvious and costly, and the assessment work itself is embodied, conducted in person with continuous physiological monitoring. No current deployment realistically substitutes for a trained practitioner physically present with an at-risk client. The binding constraint is this combination of high verification burden and embodiment, which keeps near-term exposure minimal.

By 2031 AI clinical-decision-support tools may assist with flagging contraindications or drafting baseline prescription templates for common special-population profiles, marginally raising realized task automatability, but the course's core instrumental function, safely assessing and monitoring medically complex individuals during exertion and adjusting in real time, remains resistant. Task-exposure research notes that science and critical-thinking-intensive work is negatively associated with exposure, and interpreting how a neurological or cardiovascular condition interacts with acute exercise stress is exactly this kind of judgment-heavy, non-templated reasoning. Productivity gains documented elsewhere skew toward lower-skill, well-defined tasks, not toward high-stakes individualized clinical judgment. Embodiment and verification burden both remain protective at this horizon; the special-population focus of this course is precisely what current evidence suggests resists automation longest, even as adjacent general-population fitness assessment grows more exposed.

Projecting to 2036 is necessarily uncertain, but even generous extrapolation from capability trends does not overcome the two compounding protections here: physical, real-time monitoring of at-risk clients during testing, and the high cost of an unverified error in a cardiac, neurological, or prenatal context. Macro-level productivity estimates (Acemoglu) suggest modest aggregate effects from AI over a decade, and adoption diffusion (Census BTOS) remains uneven across sectors, with healthcare-adjacent, liability-sensitive fields typically lagging. It is plausible that AI-assisted decision support becomes a standard adjunct tool practitioners consult, but that changes practice, not the instrumental need for a human trained to assess, monitor, and intervene with medically complex clients in person. This course's rating stays low across the full window; nothing in the evidence palette supports a confident higher-exposure claim here.
EXS 4790.d: Students in this course will be introduced to the unique exercise requirements for individuals with chronic health conditions as well as those with special considerations. The importance of physical activity and fitness will be explored in common disease states and conditions. Emphasis will be placed on special considerations for exercise assessment and prescription in common conditions and diseases, such as but not limited to cardiovascular, metabolic, neurological, aging, and pregnancy.

r: Biomechanics of Human Movement teaches the mechanical analysis of human motion, stability, force, and leverage as applied to movement patterns and motor-performance optimization. This is quantitative, analytical coursework, closer to applied physics than to hands-on clinical assessment, with force calculations, kinematic and kinetic analysis performed largely on paper or in software. Task-exposure research finds science and critical-thinking-intensive skills strongly negatively associated with exposure, which is directly relevant to the interpretive reasoning this course teaches, distinguishing it from more templated writing tasks. Current AI tools can already assist with mechanical calculations and biomechanical modeling, but Anthropic Economic Index data situates that assistance within the broader Computer and Mathematical usage category rather than showing wholesale task replacement. Near-term exposure is real but limited: computational sub-tasks are assisted, the underlying analytical and modeling competency the course builds is not yet substituted.

By 2031, computational biomechanical analysis, force calculations, movement modeling, leverage-principle applications, plausibly becomes substantially AI-assisted, since these are structured, formalizable problems well within the kind of task where GitHub Copilot-style productivity gains and jagged-frontier competence have already been demonstrated for analogous quantitative work. The course's realized task automatability rises accordingly. Verification burden remains meaningful, however: applying mechanical analysis correctly to real human movement, especially where conclusions inform injury risk or rehabilitation, still benefits from an expert checking AI output against physical plausibility and individual variation, consistent with the negative association between critical-thinking-intensive work and exposure found in task-exposure research. The net effect is a course whose computational content is increasingly automatable while its judgment-intensive application to real bodies keeps full instrumental displacement in check at this horizon.

At the ten-year horizon, capability-trend extrapolation (METR/Epoch doubling times) makes it plausible that AI systems competently perform most formal biomechanical analysis and modeling tasks with limited need for a human to execute the calculations directly, and GDPval-style benchmarks already show top models approaching expert parity on realistic analytical deliverables. But this is a hedge rather than a forecast: verification burden does not disappear, since applying biomechanical conclusions to injury prevention or performance optimization for real individuals still carries error costs that plausibly require expert review of AI-generated analysis, which caps the rating below full automation. Diffusion remains uneven per BTOS data, and the course's analytical, non-formulaic reasoning core keeps the instrumental need for trained human judgment from disappearing, even as the mechanics of computation are largely offloaded.

r: The Exercise Science internship is a ten-credit, culminating field placement in which students work directly with fitness, wellness, and healthcare professionals in community settings, applying the accumulated coursework of the major under live supervision. This is the most embodied, in-person course in the sequence: professional socialization, supervised client interaction, real-time judgment under mentorship, and workplace-specific practice cannot be replicated remotely. Task-exposure research explicitly classifies manual and physically co-located work as low-exposure, and that classification applies squarely here regardless of how automatable any individual documentation or administrative sub-task at the internship site becomes. Observed-usage data shows AI concentrated in office and computer-based work, not in supervised professional field placement. The binding constraint is structural: the internship's instrumental purpose is embodied, mentored, real-world practice, which by definition cannot be substituted by a model performing tasks elsewhere.

By 2031, AI tools will likely handle more of the administrative periphery around an internship, documentation, scheduling, client-record summarization, at whatever site a student is placed, modestly raising realized automatability of ancillary tasks. But the course's instrumental core does not shift: students are required to be physically present, supervised, and evaluated performing professional work with real clients and professionals, and no plausible AI deployment substitutes for that experiential requirement. Diffusion data indicates AI adoption remains uneven across the wellness and healthcare-adjacent employers where these placements occur, further slowing any indirect effect. Embodiment and verification (a supervising professional evaluates the student's judgment directly) both stay protective. The hedge here is narrow: administrative sub-tasks embedded in the internship experience may be increasingly AI-assisted, but the placement's defining requirement remains resistant to substitution at this horizon.

Even with a full decade of compounding capability growth, the internship's instrumental function, supervised, embodied, real-world professional practice as the culminating requirement of the major, has no clear substitution path in the evidence available. Macro-level estimates of AI's aggregate productivity effect over a decade remain modest, and nothing in current capability or diffusion trends addresses the specific requirement this course fulfills: physical presence at a community fitness, wellness, or healthcare site under professional supervision. It is conceivable that AI tools further automate documentation, client tracking, or program administration at internship sites, but that changes how the placement's ancillary tasks are performed, not whether the placement itself remains necessary. This course's rating stays low across all three horizons; the evidence palette offers no basis for projecting meaningful erosion of its embodied, experiential core.
